claim: The adult C. elegans male nervous system comprises 387 neurons, of which 93 are male-specific.
source: This updates the anatomy of the adult C. elegans male: it now comprises 387 neurons (93 of which are male-specific) and 90 glia (two are lost during the transdifferentiation to the PHDs).
evidence: This is stated as a result of the discovery of PHD neurons through transdifferentiation.

claim: The adult C. elegans male has 90 glia, with two lost during transdifferentiation to PHDs.
source: This updates the anatomy of the adult C. elegans male: it now comprises 387 neurons (93 of which are male-specific) and 90 glia (two are lost during the transdifferentiation to the PHDs).
evidence: This is stated as a result of the discovery that PHso1 cells transdifferentiate into neurons.

claim: PHso1 cells undergo glia-to-neuron transdifferentiation in males during sexual maturation.
source: We find that during sexual maturation (L4 stage), the pair of sex-shared PHso1 glial cells acquire sexually dimorphic function by undergoing a direct (without cell division) glia-to-neuron transdifferentiation that results in the generation of male-specific neurons, which we term the phasmid D neurons (PHDs).
evidence: This is supported by morphological observations, marker expression changes, and time-lapse imaging during the L4 stage.

claim: PHso1-to-PHD transdifferentiation occurs during the L4 larval stage.
source: We find that during this stage PHso1 retracts its socket process and extends a short dendrite-like posterior projection into the PHsh cell and a long axon-like anterior process projecting towards the pre-anal ganglion region.
evidence: Time-lapse imaging shows the morphological changes occur during L4 stage.

claim: Socket retraction in PHso1 is initiated at early L4 when the male gonad has almost reached the tail.
source: A time-lapse of an individual male reveals that socket retraction is initiated at early L4, when the male gonad has almost reached the tail, and that the nascent axon is first observed at mid-L4, when the vas deferens has joined with the cloaca (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated through time-lapse imaging of individual males.

claim: The nascent axon in PHso1 is first observed at mid-L4 when the vas deferens has joined with the cloaca.
source: A time-lapse of an individual male reveals that socket retraction is initiated at early L4, when the male gonad has almost reached the tail, and that the nascent axon is first observed at mid-L4, when the vas deferens has joined with the cloaca (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated through time-lapse imaging of individual males.

claim: PHso1 cells express the panglial microRNA mir-228 in adult hermaphrodites.
source: In adult hermaphrodites, we find that both cells express the panglial microRNA mir-228 (Wallace et al., 2016) and the AMso and PHso glial subtype marker grl-2 (a Hedgehog-like and Ground-like gene protein: Hao et al., 2006) at similar levels (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is shown using reporter transgenes and cited references.

claim: PHso1 cells express the glial subtype marker grl-2 in adult hermaphrodites.
source: In adult hermaphrodites, we find that both cells express the panglial microRNA mir-228 (Wallace et al., 2016) and the AMso and PHso glial subtype marker grl-2 (a Hedgehog-like and Ground-like gene protein: Hao et al., 2006) at similar levels (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is shown using reporter transgenes and cited references.

claim: In males, mir-228 expression is noticeably dimmer in PHso1 than in PHso2 by mid-to-late L4 stage.
source: In males, by contrast, mir-228 and grl-2 expression is noticeably dimmer in PHso1 than in PHso2 by the mid-to-late L4 stage and completely absent by day 2 of adulthood (Figure 3A, B and C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through reporter transgene expression analysis.

claim: In males, grl-2 expression is noticeably dimmer in PHso1 than in PHso2 by mid-to-late L4 stage.
source: In males, by contrast, mir-228 and grl-2 expression is noticeably dimmer in PHso1 than in PHso2 by the mid-to-late L4 stage and completely absent by day 2 of adulthood (Figure 3A, B and C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through reporter transgene expression analysis.

claim: mir-228 and grl-2 expression is completely absent in PHso1 by day 2 of adulthood in males.
source: In males, by contrast, mir-228 and grl-2 expression is noticeably dimmer in PHso1 than in PHso2 by the mid-to-late L4 stage and completely absent by day 2 of adulthood (Figure 3A, B and C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through reporter transgene expression analysis.

claim: PHso1 begins to express the pan-neuronal marker rab-3 in males after posterior hypodermal cells begin to retract.
source: After the posterior hypodermal cells begin to retract leaving the characteristic fluid-filled extracellular space at the tail, PHso1 begins to express the pan-neuronal marker rab-3 (a synaptic vesicle associated Ras GTPase: Stefanakis et al., 2015) in males but not in hermaphrodites, and this expression persists throughout adulthood (Figure 3A, B and C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through reporter transgene expression analysis and cited references.

claim: PHso1 does not express rab-3 in hermaphrodites.
source: After the posterior hypodermal cells begin to retract leaving the characteristic fluid-filled extracellular space at the tail, PHso1 begins to express the pan-neuronal marker rab-3 (a synaptic vesicle associated Ras GTPase: Stefanakis et al., 2015) in males but not in hermaphrodites, and this expression persists throughout adulthood (Figure 3A, B and C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through reporter transgene expression analysis.

claim: PHD neurons express the vesicle acetylcholine transporter unc-17.
source: In addition to rab-3 expression we also observe sequential expression of other neuronal markers such as: the vesicle acetylcholine transporter unc-17 (Alfonso et al., 1993; Pereira et al., 2015; Figure 3D)
evidence: This is demonstrated through reporter transgene expression and cited references.

claim: PHD neurons express the phogrin orthologue ida-1 for dense-core vesicle secretion.
source: In addition to rab-3 expression we also observe sequential expression of other neuronal markers such as: the vesicle acetylcholine transporter unc-17 (Alfonso et al., 1993; Pereira et al., 2015; Figure 3D); the phogrin orthologue for dense-core vesicle secretion ida-1 (Zahn et al., 2001; Figure 3E)
evidence: This is demonstrated through reporter transgene expression and cited references.

claim: PHD neurons express the intraflagellar transport component osm-6 required for proper sensory cilium structure.
source: In addition to rab-3 expression we also observe sequential expression of other neuronal markers such as: the vesicle acetylcholine transporter unc-17 (Alfonso et al., 1993; Pereira et al., 2015; Figure 3D); the phogrin orthologue for dense-core vesicle secretion ida-1 (Zahn et al., 2001; Figure 3E); the intraflagellar transport component required for proper sensory cilium structure osm-6 (Collet et al., 1998; Figure 3F)
evidence: This is demonstrated through reporter transgene expression and cited references.

claim: PHD neurons express the IG domain containing protein oig-8.
source: In addition to rab-3 expression we also observe sequential expression of other neuronal markers such as: the vesicle acetylcholine transporter unc-17 (Alfonso et al., 1993; Pereira et al., 2015; Figure 3D); the phogrin orthologue for dense-core vesicle secretion ida-1 (Zahn et al., 2001; Figure 3E); the intraflagellar transport component required for proper sensory cilium structure osm-6 (Collet et al., 1998; Figure 3F); and the IG domain containing protein oig-8 (Howell and Hobert, 2017; Figure 6A).
evidence: This is demonstrated through reporter transgene expression and cited references.

claim: PHso2 does not express neuronal markers unc-17, ida-1, osm-6, or oig-8.
source: None of these neuronal markers are observed in PHso2 or in the hermaphrodite PHso1.
evidence: This is stated as a negative result from marker expression analysis.

claim: Hermaphrodite PHso1 does not express neuronal markers unc-17, ida-1, osm-6, or oig-8.
source: None of these neuronal markers are observed in PHso2 or in the hermaphrodite PHso1.
evidence: This is stated as a negative result from marker expression analysis.

claim: PHD neurons are cholinergic.
source: Together, these data demonstrate that the male PHso1 bilateral pair of glial cells transdifferentiate into a novel class of cholinergic and likely peptidergic ciliated neurons, which we have termed phasmid D neurons (PHDs).
evidence: This is inferred from unc-17 expression, which is a vesicle acetylcholine transporter.

claim: PHD neurons are likely peptidergic.
source: Together, these data demonstrate that the male PHso1 bilateral pair of glial cells transdifferentiate into a novel class of cholinergic and likely peptidergic ciliated neurons, which we have termed phasmid D neurons (PHDs).
evidence: This is inferred from ida-1 expression, which is involved in dense-core vesicle secretion.

claim: PHD neurons are ciliated.
source: Together, these data demonstrate that the male PHso1 bilateral pair of glial cells transdifferentiate into a novel class of cholinergic and likely peptidergic ciliated neurons, which we have termed phasmid D neurons (PHDs).
evidence: This is supported by osm-6 expression and ultrastructural observations of cilia.

claim: PHso1-to-PHD transdifferentiation is mainly direct without cell division.
source: In the majority of cases (79% of sides scored), no EdU signal was detected, indicating that PHso1 mainly transdifferentiates directly into the PHD neuron.
evidence: This is demonstrated through EdU staining experiments.

claim: In 21% of cases, PHso1 divides symmetrically to give rise to two neurons termed PHD1 and PHD2.
source: In 21% of sides however, EdU signal was detected in two lin-48prom::tdTomato-expressing cells per side in the tail of male animals (Figure 3G) but never in hermaphrodites (data not shown).
evidence: This is demonstrated through EdU staining experiments.

claim: PHso1 division to produce PHD1 and PHD2 never occurs in hermaphrodites.
source: In 21% of sides however, EdU signal was detected in two lin-48prom::tdTomato-expressing cells per side in the tail of male animals (Figure 3G) but never in hermaphrodites (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated as a negative result from EdU staining experiments.

claim: There is no cell death in the PHso1 lineage.
source: We observe no statistically significant increase in the frequency of 'survivor cells' in ced-4(n1162) mutants compared to controls, when scoring the number of cells per side of each animal. This suggests there is no cell death in the PHso1 lineage (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated through analysis of ced-4 mutants that block apoptosis.

claim: PHso1-to-PHD transdifferentiation is regulated by the genetic sex of the cell in a cell-autonomous manner.
source: We find that fem-3 expression specifically in the PHso1, and not PHso2, transforms PHso1 into a PHD-like neuron, resulting in the upregulation of ida-1 and rab-3 expression and the acquisition of neuronal morphology (Figure 4A–C). This indicates that the competence of PHso1 to transdifferentiate into PHD is likely cell-intrinsic and based on genetic sex.
evidence: This is demonstrated through cell-specific masculinization experiments using fem-3 expression.

claim: Expression of fem-3 in hermaphrodite PHso1 transforms it into a PHD-like neuron.
source: We find that fem-3 expression specifically in the PHso1, and not PHso2, transforms PHso1 into a PHD-like neuron, resulting in the upregulation of ida-1 and rab-3 expression and the acquisition of neuronal morphology (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through cell-specific masculinization experiments.

claim: Expression of fem-3 in hermaphrodite PHso2 does not transform it into a neuron.
source: We find that fem-3 expression specifically in the PHso1, and not PHso2, transforms PHso1 into a PHD-like neuron, resulting in the upregulation of ida-1 and rab-3 expression and the acquisition of neuronal morphology (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This is stated as a negative result from cell-specific masculinization experiments.

claim: sem-4 is not required for PHso1-to-PHD transdifferentiation.
source: We observed no statistically significant defect in the number and cell identity of MCM and PHD neurons in sem-4(n1971) null mutants (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is demonstrated through analysis of sem-4 null mutants.

claim: egl-27 affects the division pattern of the T lineage and consequently the production of PHso1.
source: No lin-48prom::tdTomato expression is ever observed in the region of PHso1/PHD in egl-27 mutants at any stage or in either sex (Figure 5A and data not shown). This is consistent with previous results that show that egl-27 affects the division pattern of the T lineage and consequently the production of PHso1 (Herman et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated based on current observations and cited previous results.

claim: sox-2 has an early role in an unknown lineage to suppress the production of supernumerary AMso cells.
source: This, together with the fact that ectopic lin-48-positive cells are induced in RNAi-treated animals only in the F1 generation (and not the P0 generation – see Materials and methods), suggests an early role of sox-2 in an unknown lineage to supress the production of supernumerary AMso cells.
evidence: This is inferred from RNAi experiments showing ectopic AMso cells.

claim: sox-2 is not required for PHso1-to-PHD transdifferentiation.
source: No statistically significant defect is observed in the PHD neuron in sox-2 RNAi-treated animals (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is demonstrated through RNAi knockdown experiments.

claim: Factors required for Y-to-PDA transdifferentiation are largely dispensable for PHso1-to-PHD transdifferentiation.
source: Mutants in the same genes implicated in Y-to-PDA transdifferentiation were employed in this work and with the exception of sox-2, identical alleles were used. However, while the Y cell completely fails to transdifferentiate into PDA in these mutants (70–100% of the cases - Kagias et al., 2012), the PHso1-to-PHD and AMso-to-AMso+MCM cell fate switches show no or only very mild defects. Altogether these results suggest that different molecular mechanisms from the ones regulating Y-to-PDA must govern the PHso1-to-PHD and AMso-to-AMso+MCM cell fate switches.
evidence: This is demonstrated through comparison of mutant phenotypes with cited previous work.

claim: PHD neurons form synapses in the pre-anal ganglion.
source: Expression of a rab-3 translational fusion under the control of this oig-8 promoter reveals that PHDs form synapses in the pre-anal ganglion, where the synaptic vesicle associated mCherry-tagged RAB-3 protein can be observed (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is demonstrated through expression of a synaptic marker.

claim: PHD neurons contain synaptic vesicles and dense-core vesicles proximal to the cell body.
source: At the ultrastructural level, we observed both synaptic and dense-core vesicles in PHD, proximal to the cell body (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is demonstrated through electron microscopy.

claim: PHD neurons have cilia including basal body and axonemes.
source: Ultrastructural analysis of the PHD dendrite in seven different animals independently confirms John Sulston's original observation on the presence of cilia, including the basal body and axonemes (Sulston et al., 1980).
evidence: This is demonstrated through electron microscopy and confirms previous observations.

claim: The PHD basal body lies just dorsal and anterior to the phasmid sheath channel containing the PHA and PHB cilia.
source: The basal body of PHD lies just dorsal and anterior to the phasmid sheath channel containing the PHA and PHB cilia.
evidence: This is demonstrated through ultrastructural analysis.

claim: PHD has 2, 1, or 0 short cilia extending within the phasmid sheath very close to PHA and PHB cilia.
source: It has 2, 1, or 0 short cilia extending within the phasmid sheath very close to PHA and PHB cilia, but within a separate sheath channel.
evidence: This is demonstrated through ultrastructural analysis.

claim: PHD dendrite has unciliated finger-like villi within the phasmid sheath cell, proximal to the basal body.
source: In addition, we observe that the dendrite is more elaborate than previously described and has a number of unciliated finger-like villi within the phasmid sheath cell, proximal to the basal body (Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated through ultrastructural analysis.

claim: PHD neurons receive synaptic input from male-specific ray sensory neurons.
source: PHDs receive synaptic input from male-specific ray sensory neurons involved in the initiation of the mating sequence in response to mate contact (Barr and Sternberg, 1999; Liu and Sternberg, 1995; Koo et al., 2011).
evidence: This is demonstrated through electron microscopy reconstruction and cited references.

claim: The main PHD output is to the male-specific EF interneurons, representing 35.4% of chemical synapses.
source: The main PHD output is to the male-specific EF interneurons (35.4% of chemical synapses), both directly and through their second major post-synaptic target, the sex-shared PVN interneuron.
evidence: This is demonstrated through electron microscopy reconstruction.

claim: PHD neurons synapse onto the sex-shared PVN interneuron.
source: The main PHD output is to the male-specific EF interneurons (35.4% of chemical synapses), both directly and through their second major post-synaptic target, the sex-shared PVN interneuron.
evidence: This is demonstrated through electron microscopy reconstruction.

claim: EF interneurons are GABAergic and synapse onto AVB pre-motor interneurons which drive forward locomotion.
source: The EF interneurons are GABAergic (Serrano-Saiz et al., 2017b) and synapse onto the AVB pre-motor interneurons which drive forward locomotion.
evidence: This is stated based on cited references and connectivity analysis.

claim: PHD neurons synapse onto PVV and PDB interneurons which synapse onto body-wall muscle.
source: Other PHD outputs include the PVV (male-specific) and PDB (sex-shared but highly dimorphic in connectivity; Jarrell et al., 2012; Cook et al., 2019) interneurons, which synapse onto body-wall muscle
evidence: This is demonstrated through electron microscopy reconstruction and cited references.

claim: PHD neurons synapse onto cholinergic male-specific interneurons PVY and PVX whose output is to AVA pre-motor interneurons.
source: Other PHD outputs include the PVV (male-specific) and PDB (sex-shared but highly dimorphic in connectivity; Jarrell et al., 2012; Cook et al., 2019) interneurons, which synapse onto body-wall muscle, and the cholinergic male-specific interneurons PVY and PVX whose output is to the AVA pre-motor interneurons, which drive backward locomotion.
evidence: This is demonstrated through electron microscopy reconstruction.

claim: AVA pre-motor interneurons drive backward locomotion.
source: Other PHD outputs include the PVV (male-specific) and PDB (sex-shared but highly dimorphic in connectivity; Jarrell et al., 2012; Cook et al., 2019) interneurons, which synapse onto body-wall muscle, and the cholinergic male-specific interneurons PVY and PVX whose output is to the AVA pre-motor interneurons, which drive backward locomotion.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: PHD neurons may be proprioceptive neurons that respond directly to internal cues arising from muscle contractions.
source: Together, these results suggest that PHDs may respond directly to internal cues arising from muscle contractions, and that they may be proprioceptive neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from calcium imaging experiments showing activity in response to muscle contractions.

claim: PHD neurons show intermittent calcium transients in restrained animals without exogenous stimulation.
source: To our surprise, without applying any exogenous stimulation, we observed intermittent calcium transients in the PHDs of wildtype animals, every 30 s on average (Figure 6E–F and Video 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated through calcium imaging in restrained animals.

claim: Inhibition of muscle activity reduces calcium transients in PHD neurons.
source: Histamine-treated myo-3prom::HisCl1;unc-51(e369) animals were highly immobile and the frequency of calcium transients in the PHDs was strongly reduced (Figure 6E–F and Videos 2 and 3). Transients were completely eliminated in half of the neurons (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is demonstrated through calcium imaging with inducible muscle silencing.

claim: PHD activity does not require chemical input from the network.
source: In both these mutants, PHD calcium transients persisted at similar frequencies to those in wildtype animals (Figure 6E and F). This suggests that PHD activity does not require chemical input from the network.
evidence: This is demonstrated through calcium imaging in unc-13 and unc-31 mutants.

claim: PHD neurons may sense internal tissue deformations through their elaborate ciliated dendrites.
source: PHDs may sense internal tissue deformations through their elaborate ciliated dendrites, which are deeply encased in the phasmid sheath and not exposed to the outside environment.
evidence: This is inferred from the morphology and location of PHD dendrites.

claim: A novel readjustment movement termed the 'Molina manoeuvre' occurs when males have difficulty inserting spicules and lose vulva apposition.
source: During our behavioural analysis of wildtype males, we identified a novel readjustment movement that has not been previously described which we have termed the 'Molina manoeuvre'. This movement occurs when the male has been trying to insert its spicules in the mate's vulva for a period of time without success and subsequently loses vulva apposition.
evidence: This is a novel observation from behavioral analysis.

claim: The Molina manoeuvre consists of forward locomotion away from the vulva followed by backward locomotion returning to the vulva.
source: The Molina manoeuvre consists of the initiation of forward locomotion along the mate's body away from the vulva to the end of the mate's body (or at least two male tail-tips distance away from the vulva), at which point the male tail acquires a deeply arched posture, followed by a return to the vulva with backward locomotion along the same route (Video 5).
evidence: This is demonstrated through behavioral observation and video recording.

claim: Small displacements from the vulva lead to Molina manoeuvres in 32% of vulva losses.
source: We find that these small displacements from the vulva lead either to local shifts to relocate the vulva (68% of total vulva losses) or to a Molina manoeuvre (32% of vulva losses) (Figure 7).
evidence: This is demonstrated through quantitative behavioral analysis.

claim: PHD-ablated males perform fewer continuous backward scans during vulva search compared to intact males.
source: PHD-ablated males often switched their direction of locomotion during scanning, performing fewer continuous backward scans during vulva search compared to intact males (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through behavioral analysis of ablated males.

claim: PHD activity is higher during backward locomotion than during forward locomotion while scanning.
source: Consistent with this, we observed higher activity (i.e. Ca2+ levels) in PHD during backward locomotion than during forward locomotion while scanning (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through calcium imaging during mating behavior.

claim: PHD activity peaks just after the switch to backward locomotion during Molina manoeuvres.
source: PHD activity also peaked just after the switch to backward locomotion during Molina manoeuvres, when the tail tip displays an acute bent posture
evidence: This is demonstrated through calcium imaging during mating behavior.

claim: PHD-ablated males performed defective, discontinuous Molina manoeuvres, often stopping at the transition from forward to backward locomotion.
source: PHD activity also peaked just after the switch to backward locomotion during Molina manoeuvres, when the tail tip displays an acute bent posture, and PHD-ablated males performed defective, discontinuous manoeuvres, often stopping at the transition from forward to backward locomotion to return to the vulva (Figure 7F and Video 7).
evidence: This is demonstrated through behavioral analysis of ablated males.

claim: PHD neurons are not required for the initiation of Molina manoeuvres.
source: Importantly, we did not find significant differences between intact and PHD-ablated males in number of events that trigger the initiation of manoeuvres (Figure 7G), indicating that PHDs are specifically required for coordinated locomotion during the manoeuvre itself, at the transition point to backward locomotion.
evidence: This is demonstrated through behavioral analysis of ablated males.

claim: Acute silencing of PHD neurons with HisCl1 results in discontinuous Molina manoeuvres similar to ablation.
source: Similar locomotion defects resulting in discontinuous manoeuvres were observed when PHD neurons were acutely silenced with an inducible chloride channel transgene (oig-8prom::HisCl1::sl2::rfp) (Figure 7G).
evidence: This is demonstrated through behavioral analysis with inducible silencing.

claim: The highest level of PHD activation is observed during intromission.
source: In addition to the aforementioned changes in neuronal activity, the highest level of PHD activation was observed during intromission, the penultimate step of the mating sequence, which precedes sperm transfer and involves full insertion of the spicules into the mate's vulva while sustaining backward locomotion.
evidence: This is demonstrated through calcium imaging during mating behavior.

claim: PHD activity increases two-fold upon spicule insertion and remains high for several seconds.
source: PHD activity increased two-fold upon spicule insertion and remained high for several seconds while the spicules were inserted (Figure 7H).
evidence: This is demonstrated through calcium imaging during mating behavior.

claim: PHD-ablated males that complete mating produce fewer cross-progeny than intact males.
source: PHDs are required for the efficiency of these two last steps of mating since PHD-ablated males that were observed to complete the mating sequence, including intromission and ejaculation, during a single mating with one individual mate, produced fewer cross-progeny than intact males in the same conditions (Figure 7H).
evidence: This is demonstrated through fertility assays of ablated males.

claim: PHD neurons are not required for food-leaving behavior.
source: We found no defects in food-leaving behaviour, response to mate contact, turning, location of vulva, or spicule insertion (Figure 7A,B,D,E and H).
evidence: This is stated as a negative result from behavioral analysis of ablated males.

claim: PHD neurons are not required for response to mate contact.
source: We found no defects in food-leaving behaviour, response to mate contact, turning, location of vulva, or spicule insertion (Figure 7A,B,D,E and H).
evidence: This is stated as a negative result from behavioral analysis of ablated males.

claim: PHD neurons are not required for turning during mating.
source: We found no defects in food-leaving behaviour, response to mate contact, turning, location of vulva, or spicule insertion (Figure 7A,B,D,E and H).
evidence: This is stated as a negative result from behavioral analysis of ablated males.

claim: PHD neurons are not required for location of vulva.
source: We found no defects in food-leaving behaviour, response to mate contact, turning, location of vulva, or spicule insertion (Figure 7A,B,D,E and H).
evidence: This is stated as a negative result from behavioral analysis of ablated males.

claim: PHD neurons are not required for spicule insertion.
source: We found no defects in food-leaving behaviour, response to mate contact, turning, location of vulva, or spicule insertion (Figure 7A,B,D,E and H).
evidence: This is stated as a negative result from behavioral analysis of ablated males.

claim: This is the second example of neurons arising from glia in C. elegans.
source: This is the second example of neurons arising from glia in C. elegans, confirming that glia can act as neural progenitors across metazoan taxa.
evidence: This is stated as a comparison to the previously described AMso-to-MCM case.

claim: Fully differentiated, functional glia can retain neural progenitor properties during normal development in C. elegans.
source: In both cases we have demonstrated that fully differentiated, functional glia can retain neural progenitor properties during normal development.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the current work and previous work on AMso.

claim: PHso1-to-PHD is the second direct transdifferentiation to be described in C. elegans.
source: In contrast, the work described here characterises a direct transdifferentiation and as such is the second direct transdifferentiation to be described in C. elegans.
evidence: This is stated as a comparison to Y-to-PDA transdifferentiation.

claim: Y-to-PDA transdifferentiation occurs in hermaphrodites at the late L1 stage.
source: As with PHso1-to-PHD, Y-to-PDA occurs directly, without a division and in a sex-specific manner. However, Y-to-PDA happens exclusively in hermaphrodites (in males the Y blast cell divides and PDA is generated from the anterior daughter of this division) and during the late L1 stage, much earlier than sexual maturation.
evidence: This is stated as background information with implicit citation to previous work.

claim: Direct conversion of glial-like neural stem cells has been observed in the adult zebrafish brain.
source: Intriguingly, direct conversion of glial-like neural stem cells has been observed in the adult zebrafish brain (Barbosa et al., 2015), suggesting that this may be a conserved mechanism for post-embryonic generation of neurons.
evidence: This is stated with a citation to suggest evolutionary conservation.

claim: The only other neurons known to be variable in their generation are the post-embryonic and male-specific DX3/4 and EF3/4 interneurons.
source: The only other neurons known to be variable in their generation are the post-embryonic and male-specific DX3/4 and EF3/4 interneurons located in the pre-anal ganglion (Sulston et al., 1983).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to previous work.

claim: EF neurons are the main post-synaptic partners of PHD.
source: It is intriguing that the EF neurons are the main post-synaptic partners of PHD (Figure 6D), and as such it is tempting to speculate there may be a possible link between cell division and cell connectivity.
evidence: This is demonstrated through electron microscopy reconstruction.

claim: PHDs may ensure sustained backward locomotion through excitation of their post-synaptic targets PVY, PVX, and EF interneurons.
source: PHDs may ensure sustained backward locomotion through excitation of their post-synaptic targets PVY, PVX, and EF interneurons, all of which have been shown to promote backward movement through AVA and AVB during scanning and location of vulva (Sherlekar and Lints, 2014; Sherlekar et al., 2013).
evidence: This is inferred from connectivity and cited functional studies of post-synaptic targets.

claim: Sensory input from the mating partner is essential for successful mating.
source: Sensory input from the mating partner is essential for successful mating and accordingly, many sensory neurons in copulation circuits are dedicated to this purpose (reviewed in Villella and Hall, 2008 and Barr et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to reviews.

claim: Coordinated motor control in all animals requires proprioception.
source: However, coordinated motor control in all animals also requires proprioception, sensory feedback from internal tissues that inform the individual about its posture and strength exerted during movement (Sherrington, 1907; Tuthill and Azim, 2018).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: The spicule neuron SPC has been attributed a putative proprioceptive role based on dendrite attachment to the base of spicules.
source: Within the male copulation circuit, a putative proprioceptive role has been attributed only to the spicule neuron SPC, on the basis of the attachment of its dendrite to the base of the spicules (Sulston et al., 1980).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to previous work.

claim: The SPC neuron is required for full spicule protraction during intromission.
source: The SPC neuron is required for full spicule protraction during intromission (García et al., 2001; Liu and Sternberg, 1995).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous work.

claim: Mechanosensory neurons are found in the mating circuits of several organisms.
source: In this light, it would be interesting to determine whether the mechanosensory neurons found in the mating circuits of several other organisms (Liu et al., 2007; Ng and Kopp, 2008; Pavlou et al., 2016) may play a role in self-sensory feedback.
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous work in other organisms.

claim: Glia-to-neuron transdifferentiation represents an extreme form of sexual dimorphism acquired by differentiated sex-shared glial cells during sexual maturation.
source: The glia-to-neuron transdifferentiation that results in PHD represents an extreme form of sexual dimorphism acquired by differentiated sex-shared glial cells during sexual maturation.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the work.

claim: PHD neurons enable smooth and coordinated readjustment of the male's movement along its mate when spicule insertion becomes difficult.
source: The PHD neurons, perhaps through proprioception, enable the smooth and coordinated readjustment of the male's movement along its mate when spicule insertion becomes difficult to attain.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from behavioral and imaging experiments.

claim: The Molina manoeuvre represents an alternative step within the stereotyped mating sequence.
source: This readjustment movement represents an alternative step within the stereotyped mating sequence.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from behavioral observations.

claim: Both cell fate and innate behaviour can be plastic yet developmentally wired.
source: These findings reveal the extent to which both cell fate and innate behaviour can be plastic yet developmentally wired.
evidence: This is stated as a broad conclusion from the work.

claim: In juvenile animals at the L2 stage, PHso1 forms the primary pore in both sexes.
source: John Sulston observed that in juvenile animals (L2 stage) of both sexes, PHso1 forms the primary pore (Sulston et al., 1980; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Sulston's original observation.

claim: In adult hermaphrodites, the phasmid sensillum retains a similar structure to L2 stage.
source: At adulthood, the hermaphrodite retains a similar structure (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated with reference to a figure showing the structure.

claim: In adult males, PHso2 forms the main pore of the phasmid sensillum.
source: In males, however, it is PHso2 that forms the main pore and PHso1 was described as having retracted from the hypodermis and to protrude into the phasmid sheath (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Sulston's original observation.

claim: In adult males, PHso1 was described to contain basal bodies in the region enveloped by the phasmid sheath.
source: It was also described to contain basal bodies, a structural component of cilia, in the region enveloped by the phasmid sheath.
evidence: This is stated with citation to Sulston's original observation.

claim: Sensory neurons are the only ciliated cells in C. elegans.
source: As sensory neurons are the only ciliated cells in C. elegans (Perkins et al., 1986), this is suggestive of neuronal fate
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation.

claim: The amphid socket-glial cell (AMso) acts as a male-specific neural progenitor during sexual maturation, dividing to self-renew and generate the MCM neurons.
source: We previously showed that in the amphid sensillum (a similar organ located in the head) the amphid socket-glial cell (AMso) acts as a male-specific neural progenitor during sexual maturation, dividing to self-renew and generate the MCM neurons (Sammut et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: At the L3 stage, there are no distinguishable differences between hermaphrodite and male PHso1 cells.
source: Using a lin-48/OVO1 reporter transgene to identify and visualise the PHso1 cell bodies both before and during sexual maturation (Johnson et al., 2001; Wildwater et al., 2011), we observed no distinguishable differences between the hermaphrodite and male PHso1 cells at the L3 stage (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated through reporter transgene expression and cited references.

claim: PHso1 cells display a polarised morphology and visible socket structure in both sexes at L3 stage.
source: The PHso1 cells display a polarised morphology and a visible socket structure in both sexes.
evidence: This is demonstrated through microscopy observations.

claim: In hermaphrodites, PHso1 morphology is maintained during the transition to adulthood and cells elongate as the animal grows.
source: In hermaphrodites, this morphology is maintained during the transition to adulthood and PHso1 cells elongate as the animal grows.
evidence: This is demonstrated through microscopy observations.

claim: The axon-like outgrowth in PHso1 is complete by the end of tail-tip retraction in males.
source: The axon-like outgrowth is complete by the end of tail-tip retraction, when ray precursor cells start to fuse into the tail seam syncytium (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated through time-lapse imaging.

claim: Expression of mir-228 and grl-2 reporters appears equal in brightness in both PHso1 and PHso2 at late L3 stage in males.
source: Importantly, expression of these reporters appears equal in brightness in both cells at the late L3 stage and only becomes noticeably dimmer in PHso1 following the morphological changes, such as the retraction of the socket, that occur during the L4 stage (Figure 3B and C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated through reporter transgene expression analysis.

claim: In hermaphrodites, mir-228 and grl-2 reporters appear equal in brightness in PHso1 and PHso2 through to adulthood.
source: In contrast, in hermaphrodites, no morphological changes of PHso1 are observed and the reporters appear equal in brightness through to adulthood (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated through reporter transgene expression analysis.

claim: EdU is never present in the PHD neuron unless observed in two cells on the same side.
source: Importantly, EdU is never present in the PHD neuron unless observed in two cells on the same side, eliminating the possibility of cell death via non-apoptotic machinery, as is the case of the male linker cell (Abraham et al., 2007).
evidence: This is demonstrated through EdU staining experiments and cited reference.

claim: An extra cell co-expressing lin-48 and rab-3 was observed in 13-24% of sides in both ced-4 mutant and control animals.
source: To our surprise, we observed the presence of an extra cell that co-expressed lin-48prom::tdTomato and rab-3prom::yfp in 13–24% of sides of both ced-4 mutant and control animals (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated through marker expression analysis in mutants.

claim: The extra cell expressing PHD markers was located immediately anterior to PHD and detected from early L4 stage onwards.
source: This extra cell had a similar morphology to PHD, was located immediately anterior to PHD and was detected from the early L4 stage onwards.
evidence: This is demonstrated through microscopy observations.

claim: The percentage occurrence of the extra PHD-like cell is variable between strains suggesting its presence/absence is background-dependent.
source: We realised, however, the percentage occurrence of this extra cell was variable between strains suggesting its presence/absence is background-dependent (Figure 3—figure supplement 2H).
evidence: This is demonstrated through comparison of different strains.

claim: The division of PHso1 was observed in a time-lapse of an individual male.
source: In addition, we were able to observe the division of PHso1 in a single animal in a time-lapse of an individual male (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated through time-lapse imaging.

claim: An apoptotic cell body was never observed in the vicinity of the PHD neuron.
source: Moreover, we never observed an apoptotic cell body in the vicinity of the PHD neuron.
evidence: This is stated as a negative observation from microscopy.

claim: In egl-27 mutants, a significant defect is observed in the number of lin-48-positive MCM neurons but normal rab-3 expression suggests normal neuronal fate acquisition.
source: In egl-27(ok1671) strong loss-of-function mutants, although a significant defect is observed in the number of lin-48prom::tdTomato-positive MCM neurons, normal rab-3prom::yfp expression suggests a defect in lin-48::tdTomato reporter transgene expression levels but not in the division of the AMso or in the acquisition of neuronal fate by the MCM.
evidence: This is demonstrated through marker expression analysis in mutants.

claim: An increase in the number of rab-3-expressing MCM cells was detected in sox-2 RNAi-treated animals.
source: An increase in the number of rab-3prom::yfp-expressing MCM cells was detected (Figure 5B)
evidence: This is demonstrated through RNAi knockdown experiments.

claim: Analysis of lin-48 expression revealed that extra rab-3 positive cells in sox-2 RNAi animals derive from ectopic AMso cells that divide efficiently to produce MCM neurons.
source: An increase in the number of rab-3prom::yfp-expressing MCM cells was detected (Figure 5B) but analysis of lin-48prom::tdTomato expression revealed that the extra rab-3 positive cells derive from ectopic AMso cells that divide efficiently to produce MCM neurons (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated through marker expression analysis.

claim: Ectopic MCM cells in sox-2 RNAi animals express both rab-3 and ida-1, recapitulating normal development.
source: Interestingly, the ectopic MCM cells recapitulate normal development as they not only express the pan-neuronal marker rab-3prom::yfp, but also the neuron subtype marker ida-1prom::gfp (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated through marker expression analysis.

claim: Ectopic AMso cells in sox-2 RNAi animals are observed in both sexes but exclusively divide in males.
source: Moreover, although ectopic AMso cells are observed in both sexes, they exclusively divide in males and not in hermaphrodites (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated through marker expression analysis in both sexes.

claim: Ectopic lin-48-positive cells are induced in RNAi-treated animals only in the F1 generation and not the P0 generation.
source: This, together with the fact that ectopic lin-48-positive cells are induced in RNAi-treated animals only in the F1 generation (and not the P0 generation – see Materials and methods), suggests an early role of sox-2 in an unknown lineage to supress the production of supernumerary AMso cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated through RNAi experiments comparing P0 and F1 generations.

claim: In sox-2 null mutants rescued with a fosmid array, one ectopic ida-1-expressing MCM neuron was observed in 3/266 sides per animal.
source: In the head, one ectopic ida-1prom::gfp-expressing MCM neuron is overserved in 3/266 sides per animal, coinciding with an extra AMso (Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C) and phenocopying the F1 RNAi results.
evidence: This is demonstrated through marker expression analysis in rescued mutants.

claim: Four out of 269 total lin-48-expressing MCM cells lack ida-1 expression in sox-2 null mutants, suggesting a possible minor role of sox-2 in AMso-to-AMso+MCM.
source: However, four out of 269 total lin-48prom::tdTomato expressing MCM cells lack ida-1prom::gfp expression (Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), suggesting a possible minor role of sox-2 in AMso-to-AMso+MCM, not detected in the RNAi-knockdown experiments.
evidence: This is demonstrated through marker expression analysis in rescued mutants.

claim: PHD neurons project from the dorsolateral lumbar ganglia anteriorly and then ventrally along the posterior lumbar commissure into the pre-anal ganglion.
source: PHD neurons project from the dorsolateral lumbar ganglia anteriorly and then ventrally along the posterior lumbar commissure and into the pre-anal ganglion.
evidence: This is demonstrated through electron microscopy reconstruction.

claim: PHD neurons establish chemical synapses and gap junctions with sensory neurons and interneurons in the pre-anal ganglion, most of which are male-specific.
source: In the pre-anal ganglion, these establish chemical synapses and gap junctions with sensory neurons and interneurons, most of which are male-specific (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is demonstrated through electron microscopy reconstruction.

claim: The axonal process of PHD was previously attributed to the R8B ray neuron.
source: Previously, the axonal process of PHD was attributed to the R8B ray neuron (Jarrell et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated with citation to previous work.

claim: Re-examination of the lumbar commissure allowed disambiguation of PHD's axon from R8B.
source: A re-examination of the lumbar commissure allowed us to disambiguate PHD's axon.
evidence: This is stated as a result of the current work correcting previous attribution.

claim: PVN, PVY, and PVX form disynaptic feed-forward triplet motifs that connect PHD strongly to the locomotion circuit interneurons AVB and AVA.
source: PVN, PVY, and PVX form disynaptic feed-forward triplet motifs that connect PHD strongly to the locomotion circuit interneurons AVB and AVA.
evidence: This is demonstrated through electron microscopy reconstruction and circuit analysis.

claim: The pattern of connectivity of PHD suggests a possible role in male mating behaviour.
source: The pattern of connectivity of PHD suggests a possible role in male mating behaviour.
evidence: This is inferred from the connectivity analysis.

claim: Calcium transients were observed in 73% of PHD neurons imaged in restrained wildtype animals.
source: We observed calcium transients in 73% of the neurons imaged and no peaks could be identified in the remaining traces (n = 19).
evidence: This is demonstrated through calcium imaging experiments.

claim: Transients were completely eliminated in half of PHD neurons in histamine-treated muscle-silenced animals.
source: Histamine-treated myo-3prom::HisCl1;unc-51(e369) animals were highly immobile and the frequency of calcium transients in the PHDs was strongly reduced (Figure 6E–F and Videos 2 and 3). Transients were completely eliminated in half of the neurons (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is demonstrated through calcium imaging with muscle silencing.

claim: The reduction in PHD transient frequency was specific to muscle silencing, not to the unc-51 mutation or histamine treatment alone.
source: The reduction in transient frequency was specific to the silencing of the muscles because in histamine-treated unc-51(e369) and histamine non-treated myo-3prom::HisCl1;unc-51(e369) control animals, frequency was similar to that of wildtype animals (Figure 6E,F and Video 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated through control experiments.

claim: Unsuccessful spicule insertion attempts occurred in 65% of males.
source: Unsuccessful spicule insertion attempts occurred in 65% of males, resulting in either a long displacement from the vulva, which led to the re-initiation of the scanning sequence, or in a small displacement (less than two tail-tip length) from the vulva (98% of vulva losses), as previously described (Correa et al., 2012).
evidence: This is demonstrated through behavioral analysis and cited reference.

claim: Small displacements from the vulva lead to local shifts to relocate the vulva in 68% of total vulva losses.
source: We find that these small displacements from the vulva lead either to local shifts to relocate the vulva (68% of total vulva losses) or to a Molina manoeuvre (32% of vulva losses) (Figure 7).
evidence: This is demonstrated through quantitative behavioral analysis.

claim: Males perform the Molina manoeuvre with moving wildtype mates as well as paralysed mates.
source: Although we used paralysed unc-51 mutant hermaphrodites to aid our mating analysis, males also perform this readjustment movement with moving wildtype mates (Video 6).
evidence: This is demonstrated through behavioral observation with different mate types.

claim: Target specificity of PHD laser ablations was confirmed 1-day after ablation by absence of fluorescence returning from the transgene.
source: Target specificity of the laser ablations was confirmed 1-day after ablation by absence of fluorescence returning from the transgene used to label the PHD neurons (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is stated as a methodological validation.

claim: Ectopic prodding occurred significantly more often in PHD-ablated males than in wildtype males.
source: Ectopic prodding happened rarely but it occurred significantly more often in ablated than in wildtype males (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated through behavioral analysis of ablated males.

claim: The increase in ectopic prodding in PHD-ablated males is interpreted as a secondary consequence of pausing rather than the main defect.
source: Because ectopic prodding occurred only during pauses and PHD-ablated males produced many more discontinuous manoeuvres than wildtype males, we interpret the increase in ectopic prodding as a secondary consequence of pausing rather than as the main defect of PHD-ablated males.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the behavioral data.

claim: There was no statistically significant difference in ectopic prodding between ablated and wildtype males when only discontinuous manoeuvres were considered.
source: Consistent with this interpretation, there was no statistically significant difference in the occurrence of ectopic prodding events between ablated and wildtype males when only discontinuous manoeuvres were considered (Figure 7—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated through statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: Wildtype hermaphrodites are highly uncooperative during mating and actively move away.
source: As wildtype hermaphrodites are highly uncooperative during mating and actively move away (Kleemann and Basolo, 2007), any erratic and uncoordinated movement by the male is likely to result in the loss of its mate.
evidence: This is stated with citation to previous work.
